This paper contains six questions arranged in three sections: Section A - Physical and General Chemistry (questions 1 and 2); Section B - Inorganic Chemistry (questions 3 and 4); Section C - Organic Chemistry (questions 5 and 6).

Answer ALL the SIX questions in this booklet. The mark allocation is indicated for each question. Each question carries 20 marks. Inform the invigilator in case this booklet contains less than six questions, questions are repeated or there are blank pages so that the booklet should be changed. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. All necessary working must be shown. No marks will be awarded for answers without brief statements showing how the answers have been obtained. Calculators may be used.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Transition metals form complexes by combining with ligands. What is

(i) A transition metal?

(ii) A bidentate ligand? *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** A transition metal is a **d-block element that forms at least one stable ion with a partially filled d sub-shell** (for example $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$: $3d^9$; $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$: $3d^5$). Zinc and scandium are therefore not transition metals: $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$ is $3d^{10}$ and $\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}$ is $3d^0$.

**(ii)** A bidentate ligand is a ligand (molecule or ion) that has **two donor atoms, each with a lone pair, so that it forms two dative (co-ordinate) bonds to the same central metal ion**, giving a ring (chelate). Examples: ethane-1,2-diamine ($\mathrm{H_2NCH_2CH_2NH_2}$, "en") and the ethanedioate (oxalate) ion $\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}}$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Copper forms the hydrated complex, $[\mathrm{Cu(H_2O)_6}]^{2+}$

(i) Give the name of the complex ion and draw its shape.

(ii) Give the formula of the complex ion formed when a solution of EDTA is added to a solution of $[\mathrm{Cu(H_2O)_6}]^{2+}$

(iii) Using the s p d notation, write the electronic configuration of copper in the complex ion. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** Name: **hexaaquacopper(II) ion**. The central $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ ion is bonded to six water ligands, each donating a lone pair from oxygen through a dative bond. The shape is **octahedral** (co-ordination number 6, bond angles of 90$^\circ$):

![fig-1](gce-al-chemistry-2019-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_4_fig_1.png)

**(ii)** EDTA (as the $\mathrm{EDTA^{4-}}$ ion) is a **hexadentate** ligand (2 nitrogen and 4 oxygen donor atoms); it replaces all six water molecules:

$[\mathrm{Cu(H_2O)_6}]^{2+} + \mathrm{EDTA^{4-}} \rightarrow [\mathrm{Cu(EDTA)}]^{2-} + 6\mathrm{H_2O}$

The complex ion is **$[\mathrm{Cu(EDTA)}]^{2-}$** (charge: $+2 - 4 = -2$).

**(iii)** A copper atom is $1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6\,3d^{10}\,4s^1$. To form $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ it loses the $4s$ electron and one $3d$ electron, so the copper in the complex ion (oxidation state +2) has the configuration

$1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6\,3d^9$ (that is $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^9$).

questions.enonce_markdown:
Carbon, silicon, germanium, tin and lead are elements of Group IV (14) of the Periodic Table,

(i) State the variation in structure of the elements carbon to lead.

(ii) Give the name or formula of a chloride of Group IV element that is

A: covalent and decomposes readily at room temperature and pressure (r.t.p.).

B: strongly reducing. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The structure changes from **giant covalent (non-metallic) to giant metallic** down the group, as the metallic character increases:

- **Carbon:** giant covalent (diamond: tetrahedral lattice; graphite: layers with delocalised electrons).
- **Silicon and germanium:** giant covalent, with the diamond structure (semiconductors).
- **Tin:** grey tin has the diamond (covalent) structure; the usual white tin has a metallic lattice.
- **Lead:** giant **metallic** lattice (a typical metal).

**(ii)**

- **A: lead(IV) chloride, $\mathrm{PbCl_4}$.** It is a covalent molecular liquid (yellow oil) which is unstable and **decomposes readily** even at room temperature: $\mathrm{PbCl_4} \rightarrow \mathrm{PbCl_2} + \mathrm{Cl_2}$ (the +4 state is unstable for lead because of the inert-pair effect).
- **B: tin(II) chloride, $\mathrm{SnCl_2}$** (germanium(II) chloride $\mathrm{GeCl_2}$ also qualifies). In $\mathrm{Sn^{2+}}$ the +2 state is easily oxidised to the more stable +4 state, so $\mathrm{SnCl_2}$ is a strong reducing agent, e.g. $\mathrm{Sn^{2+}} + 2\mathrm{Fe^{3+}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Sn^{4+}} + 2\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Write an equation for the reaction of:

(i) Carbon dioxide with aqueous potassium hydroxide.

(ii) Germanium monoxide with dilute hydrochloric acid. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** Carbon dioxide is an acidic oxide and reacts with the alkali to give the carbonate (or, with excess $\mathrm{CO_2}$, the hydrogencarbonate):

$\mathrm{CO_2(g)} + 2\mathrm{KOH(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{K_2CO_3(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)}$

(with excess carbon dioxide: $\mathrm{CO_2} + \mathrm{KOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{KHCO_3}$)

**(ii)** Germanium monoxide behaves as a base towards the acid and gives germanium(II) chloride and water:

$\mathrm{GeO(s)} + 2\mathrm{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{GeCl_2(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)}$

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Give the formula of the stable oxides of the elements of Period 3 in the table below.

| Symbol of element | Na | Mg | Al | Si | P | S | Cl | Ar |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Formula of oxide | | | | | | | | |

(ii) From the table above, select an amphoteric oxide and write balanced equations to show its reactions with hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide.

Amphoteric oxide:

Reaction with HCl(aq):

Reaction with NaOH(aq):

(iii) Write an equation for the reaction of the oxide of chlorine with water. *[8 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** Stable oxides of the Period 3 elements:

| Symbol of element | Na | Mg | Al | Si | P | S | Cl | Ar |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Formula of oxide | $\mathrm{Na_2O}$ | $\mathrm{MgO}$ | $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ | $\mathrm{SiO_2}$ | $\mathrm{P_4O_{10}}$ ($\mathrm{P_2O_5}$) | $\mathrm{SO_2}$ (also $\mathrm{SO_3}$) | $\mathrm{Cl_2O_7}$ (also $\mathrm{Cl_2O}$) | none |

Argon is a noble gas and forms no oxide. (Sodium also forms the peroxide $\mathrm{Na_2O_2}$ in excess oxygen, and phosphorus the oxide $\mathrm{P_4O_6}$ in limited air.)

**(ii)** The amphoteric oxide is **aluminium oxide, $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$**: it reacts both as a base (with an acid) and as an acid (with an alkali).

- Reaction with HCl(aq): $\mathrm{Al_2O_3(s)} + 6\mathrm{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{AlCl_3(aq)} + 3\mathrm{H_2O(l)}$
- Reaction with NaOH(aq): $\mathrm{Al_2O_3(s)} + 2\mathrm{NaOH(aq)} + 3\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Na[Al(OH)_4](aq)}$ (sodium tetrahydroxoaluminate; in simplified form $\mathrm{Al_2O_3} + 2\mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NaAlO_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}$)

**(iii)** Dichlorine heptoxide, the most stable oxide of chlorine, is an acidic oxide and gives chloric(VII) (perchloric) acid, a strong acid:

$\mathrm{Cl_2O_7(l)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{HClO_4(aq)}$

(For dichlorine monoxide: $\mathrm{Cl_2O} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{HOCl}$, chloric(I) acid.)
